text:
The Conformist (1970)
****
“In individuals, insanity is rare. But in groups, parties, and nations, it is the rule.” —Friedrich Nietzsche
Any individual person isn’t going to choose to go downtown to overturn a car or torch a store. But as part of an angry mob, that same person can become an eager arsonist.
We all know that mob mentality leads to outrageous behavior. More often, mob mentality leads to outrageous beliefs.
Most people want to join a group. And once part of the group, a normal person lets the group dictate to him what is real and what is fake — what is right and what is wrong.
For example, a billion people believe that when a Priest consecrates the Host in the Eucharist, the bread literally changes form. I am not saying that they are wrong; who am I to say? I am saying that no individual — left alone to his own thoughts — would ever come up with that idea on his own. People believe it because the group believes it.
Some wonder how a person could become a suicide bomber or a cult member. I don’t. Most people have chosen to be part of some cult or another. Most people are conformists, happy to let the group decide what’s true and false.
“The Conformist” is the story of a regular guy who joins a messed-up cult: the Fascist Party in 1930s Italy. He doesn’t become a fascist because he loves war or hates democracy. He does it to conform. He does it explicitly because he craves a normal life of acceptance.
For around 1500 years, Italians had conformed to Roman Catholicism. Director Bernardo Bertolucci observes that atheism had become the norm after WWI. And rather than leading people to think for themselves, Italians just jumped to the next popular group that was telling them what to believe.
The magic of “The Conformist” is how Bertolucci looks back with nostalgia to 1930s Italy. The beautiful colors, the beautiful cars, the beautiful women: he makes interwar Italy look magical and inviting and cool. Bertolucci inspires us to love Italian culture; which makes it extra painful when we see the Blackshirts destroying it … with help from willing accomplices.
Bertolucci introduces us to an agreeable anti-hero named Marcello. Marcello is welcomed into Mussolini’s secret police and given an important mission. He is to go to Paris, find his former philosophy professor, and kill him.
Tension builds when Marcello tracks down the dissident. The professor isn’t dumb enough to think that Marcello traveled all the way from Italy to discuss Plato’s Allegory of the Cave.
The anti-fascist knows that the young fascist is there to kill him. And the professor and his wife try to kill Marcello with kindness to soften his resolve.
So will Marcello follow his heart? Or follow orders? If you view human nature like I do, you already know the answer.
Every human life is an inner conflict between wanting to be seen as an individual and the instinct to hide behind a wall of conformity. The film argues that our conformist nature almost always wins. Very few have the guts to be true individualists and come up with their own truth and their own value system. The best that most of us can do is to join a positive, loving group. There are plenty of groups out there that are stupid and awful.
